first_delegated.default_label: attribution unresolved; Wright claims the crest (his claim, documented as a claim)

basis.text: The reports of 1863 are divided in kind, not in value: Wright (28 Sep) says his brigade went to the top of the crest and withdrew because the brigade on his right gave way and none came on his left; four reports of his regiments (17-18 Jul) say the same of the withdrawal and do not name the crest; Union regiments (106th Pa., 82nd N.Y., 59th N.Y., 19th Me.) report taking the 48th Georgia's colonel and flags; no report names Wright's brigade as stopped by Webb, by Stannard or by any one unit.

default.label: No single stopper: Gibbon's regiments counter-charged and Wright's flanks gave way; the crest is Wright's claim
default.note: Three claims shown side by side: (1) Wright, Lee and Anderson say the brigade reached the top of the crest, which no other witness confirms or denies; (2) regiments of Webb's, Harrow's and Hall's brigades took the 48th Georgia's colonel and flags and checked the line at Brown's battery; (3) Wright and his four regiments say they withdrew when the brigade on their right gave way and no support came on their left. Webb, Stannard and the plan's 'stopped short of the crest' stay selectable.

positions.label: Webb: Webb's brigade (106th, 72nd, 71st, 69th Pennsylvania) turned Wright's line back

inference.step: Webb's report says his regiments fired on a line of battle that had gone beyond one gun of Brown's battery, that it halted, wavered and fell back, and that the 106th and 72nd pursued it; the 106th's colonel says his charge took Colonel Gibson of the 48th Georgia, a regiment of Wright's brigade. From this the 106th Pennsylvania of Webb's brigade is placed against Wright's left; Webb's report itself names no enemy brigade.

positions.label: Reached the crest or not: Wright says he did (his report; Lee and Anderson repeat it); his colonels and Webb do not say so

inference.step: Wright's report ('charged up to the top of the crest'), Lee's report ('Wright gained the crest') and Anderson's ('possessed themselves of the ridge') say the crest was reached; Lee and Anderson relay the brigade's own accounts. The reports of Wright's own colonels name only the enemy's 'first line', 'reserves on the height' and the batteries, and Webb puts the enemy line at one gun of Brown's battery in front of the ridge. No witness states which crest line or landmark Wright means. The claim is therefore carried as Wright's claim, not as a fact.

positions.label: No single stopper: regiments of Gibbon's division (106th Pa., 82nd N.Y., 59th N.Y., 19th Me.) counter-charged Wright's left

inference.step: Reports of the 106th Pennsylvania (Webb's brigade), the 82nd New York (Harrow's) and Hall's list of flags (59th New York, Hall's brigade) name the 48th Georgia, the left regiment of Wright's brigade, as the unit whose colonel or flags they took; Hancock credits the 19th Maine with checking the enemy at Brown's battery, and Gibbon the nearest troops and the Twelfth Corps. weighing.summary: No witness of the time says who stopped Wright's brigade as a whole. The Union reports name no Confederate brigade; they name the 48th Georgia (colonel and flags) and the regiments that took them, which belong to three brigades of Gibbon's division (Webb's, Harrow's, Hall's); Hancock and Gibbon credit the nearest troops, the 19th Maine and, further left, part of the Twelfth Corps. The 13th Vermont (Stannard) retook guns at dusk, but no report of 1863 puts it against Wright; the 1914 book names its prisoners as an Alabama regiment's. Wright and his four regimental reports agree on why he withdrew (the brigade on the right gave way, none came on the left). On the crest, only Wright's own report, with Lee and Anderson repeating it, says the top was reached; his colonels and Webb give places short of it, and nothing separates the two readings. The record is divided on the crest and not on a single stopper, so the default is a set of claims side by side.
weighing.who: Wright, Anderson and Lee wrote about their own side's advance (Lee from reports, not from the ground). The regimental colonels and captains of Wright's brigade (Walker, McCurry, Hall, Moffett) were in the line. On the Union side Curry, Darrow, Heath and Smith led the regiments in the counter-charges; Webb, Hall, Gibbon and Hancock commanded the brigades, division and corps. Stannard and Randall led the Vermonters. Wilcox, on Wright's right, wrote that he did not see Wright's brigade. Alexander gives Wright's own remark of 3 July. The Park Service handbook (1954), the study of 1981 and the books of 1904 and 1914 are later summaries, not witnesses.
weighing.when: Reports of the time: the regimental reports of both sides (11-18 July 1863, 9-16 days after), Stannard 4 July, Heath 4 July, Webb 13 July, Gibbon 7 August, Anderson 7 August, Darrow 3 August, Wright 28 September (88 days), Hancock by 24 October, Lee 20 January 1864. Later: Wilcox 1878, Alexander 1887 and 1907, the Pennsylvania address 1904, the Vermont book 1914, the Park Service 1954 and 1981. By the rubric the reports of 1863 outrank the memoirs; none of the later accounts is used to overrule a report.
weighing.where: Wright was ill on 1 July and back with the brigade at 7 a.m. on 2 July; he led the advance. His regiments' officers were in the line. Webb, Curry and Smith were in the 69th-72nd-106th line at the Angle; Darrow's 82nd New York stood at the Codori house, Heath's 19th Maine left of Brown's battery, Hall's brigade south of Webb. Stannard came up at dusk from the rear of Cemetery Hill. Gibbon commanded the corps at that hour and Hancock rode the line. Lee was far from the ground.
weighing.how_knew: Eyewitness for every regimental and brigade writer named. Lee and Anderson relay reports of the brigades. Alexander relays Wright's remark of 3 July. The later books and the Park Service summarize the reports and name the guns' captors without a source. No writer says how he knew that the Union regiment he fought was Wright's brigade; the Union writers know the 48th Georgia by its prisoners and flags.
weighing.clock: Not applicable: the question is who and where. Wright's advance began at 5 p.m. on his clock (Confederate), Lang's at 6; Webb and Heath say about 6.30 and a little past 6 on the Union clock. The 20-minute difference between the two clocks is not applied.
weighing.independence: Lines counted separately: Wright (with Lee, who repeats his report); Anderson; Walker; McCurry; Hall (48th); Moffett; Wilcox 1863; Wilcox 1878; Alexander (1887 and 1907 count once); Webb with Curry and the 1904 address (the address follows Curry); Smith; Darrow; N. J. Hall; Heath; Gibbon; Hancock; Stannard with Randall; the 1914 Vermont book; the Park Service handbook and the 1981 study. The 'who stopped it' claims of Webb and Stannard each rest on one line of evidence of the time, not two; the crest claim rests on one source (Wright) repeated by two.

source_panel_text: Unresolved. Wright's report says his Georgians reached the top of the crest; his colonels do not, and no Union report names his brigade or one stopper. 'Wright claims the crest' holds as his claim.
